Al-lahw (idle diversion) is everything that is false and that distracts one from good and from what is of concern. "Lahw al-hadith" (idle talk) includes evening chatter with fables and tales that have no basis, speaking of superstitions, jokes, superfluous speech, and whatever is unbecoming of talk of "such-and-such happened," as well as singing and learning *al-musiqar* [[His words "wa-ta'allum al-musiqar" are Greek. It is said: it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who used to trade to Persia, buying the books of the non-Arabs and relating them to the Quraysh, saying: "If Muhammad tells you the story of ʿAd and Thamud, I will tell you the stories of Rustam, Bahram, the Kisras and the kings of al-Hira." They would find his narration more pleasing and would abandon listening to the Qur'an. It is also said: he used to buy singing-girls, and whenever he found anyone who wished to embrace Islam, he would take him to his singing-girl and say: "Feed him, give him drink, and sing to him. This is better than what Muhammad calls you to: prayer, fasting, and fighting before him." There is a hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is not lawful to sell singing-girls, nor to buy them, nor to trade in them, nor to take their price." [[Mentioned earlier in Bara'ah.]] It is also permissible for the idafa to be in the sense of partitive "min," as if it were said: "Among people is one who buys some of the hadith which is idle diversion from it." One: that he would remain upon the misguidance he was upon, not turning away from it, and would increase in it and sustain it, for this forsaken one was intensely stubborn in enmity to the religion and in turning people away from it. The second: that "li-yaḍilla" is placed in the position of "li-yuḍilla," because whoever misleads is necessarily astray, so the consequence indicates what is consequent. If you ask: what is the meaning of His words "bi-ghayri ʿilm" (without knowledge)? I say: since He made him a buyer of idle talk in exchange for the Qur'an, He said: he buys without knowledge of trade and without insight into it, since he substitutes error for guidance and falsehood for truth.

And from ʿA'ishah, narrated by al-Bayhaqi, in which is Layth ibn Abi Sulaym, who is weak.]] And from him (ﷺ): "No man raises his voice in singing except that Allah sends two devils upon him, one on this shoulder and the other on that shoulder, and they keep striking him with their feet until he is the one who stops." [[Narrated by Abu Yaʿla, Ishaq and al-Harith through the route of Abu Umamah; it is in al-Tabarani through the narration of Yahya ibn al-Harith from al-Qasim in the hadith preceding it.]] It is also said: singing is a waster of wealth, a displeaser of the Lord, and a corrupter of the heart. If you ask: what is the meaning of attributing "lahw" to "hadith"? I say:

Its meaning is specification (tabyin), and this is the idafa in the sense of "min" (from), where a thing is attributed to that which it is part of, as when you say: "ṣifat khazz" (a garment of silk) and "bab sаj" (a teak door). [[His words "like your saying: ṣifat khazz and bab sāj" are probably corrupted; the original is "jubbat khazz" (a silk robe). Then I saw in al-Sihah: "ṣifat al-dar and al-sarj: singular of ṣuff", so perhaps the ṣifat of a saddle may be of silk. (ʿA).]] The meaning is: "one who buys idle talk from the hadith," because idle diversion may come from hadith and from other than it, so it is specified by "hadith." The intended "hadith" is the reprehensible talk, as in the hadith: "Talk in the mosque devours good deeds as an animal devours grass." [[Mentioned earlier in Bara'ah.]] It is also permissible for the idafa to be in the sense of partitive "min," as if it were said: "Among people is one who buys some of the hadith which is idle diversion from it." As for his words yashtari (buys), it may be from purchasing, according to what is narrated about al-Nadr: from buying the books of the non-Arabs or from buying singing-girls; or from His words "ashtaraw al-kufra bil-iman" (they exchanged disbelief for faith), meaning they substituted it and preferred it over it. It is narrated from Qatadah: its "ishtira'" is its "istihbab" (preference): he chooses the hadith of falsehood over the hadith of truth. It is read: li-yuḍilla with a damma on the ya' and with a fatha on it.

And "sabil Allah" is the religion of Islam or the Qur'an. If you ask: the reading with a damma is clear, because al-Nadr's aim in buying idle diversion was to turn people away from entering Islam and listening to the Qur'an, and to lead them astray from it; so what is the meaning of the reading with a fatha? I say: it has two meanings. One: that he would remain upon the misguidance he was upon, not turning away from it, and would increase in it and sustain it, for this forsaken one was intensely stubborn in enmity to the religion and in turning people away from it. The second: that "li-yaḍilla" is placed in the position of "li-yuḍilla," because whoever misleads is necessarily astray, so the consequence indicates what is consequent. If you ask: what is the meaning of His words "bi-ghayri ʿilm" (without knowledge)? I say: since He made him a buyer of idle talk in exchange for the Qur'an, He said: he buys without knowledge of trade and without insight into it, since he substitutes error for guidance and falsehood for truth.

Similar to this is His words: "fa-ma rabihat tijaratuhum wa-ma kanu muhtadin" (so their trade did not profit them, nor were they guided), meaning: they were not guided to trade, nor were they discerning in it. It is read "wa-yattakhidha-ha" with the accusative and the nominative, coordinated with "yashtari" or with "li-yuḍilla," and the pronoun refers to "sabil," because it is feminine, as in His words: "wa-tasuddun ʿan sabil Allah man amana bihi wa-tabghunaha ʿiwajan" (and you turn away from the way of Allah those who believe in it, seeking to make it crooked).

"Wa-lla mustakbiran" (he turns away arrogantly) with "zaman" [[His words "zaman la yaʿbaʾu biha" (scornfully, not caring for them): in al-Sihah: "zamma bi-anfihi" means he became arrogant, so he is "zamm." (ʿA).]] not caring for them and not raising his head at them: his state in that resembles the state of one who has not heard them, though he hears: "ka-anna fi udhunayhi waqran" (as if in his ears was deafness), meaning a heaviness, and there is no deafness in them. It is read with a sukun on the dhal. If you ask: what is the place of the two clauses introduced by "ka-anna"? I say: the first is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "mustakbiran," and the second from "lam yasmaʿha" (who has not heard them). It is also permissible that both be resumptive clauses (istinaf). The original in "ka-anna" (the light form) is "ka-annahu," and the pronoun is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamir al-shan).

The Qur'anic phrase "وَعْدَ اللَّهِ حَقًّا" is two emphatic verbal nouns (masdar muakkid). The first, "wa'd Allah" (the promise of God), emphasises itself, while the second, "haqqan" (truly), emphasises something other than itself. This is because His saying "لَهُمْ جَنَّاتُ النَّعِيمِ" (for them are Gardens of Bliss) carries the meaning "God has promised them the Gardens of Bliss," so the meaning of the promise is emphasised by the promise. As for "haqqan," it indicates the sense of firmness, and by it the meaning of the promise is emphasised. What emphasises both of them together is His saying "لَهُمْ جَنَّاتُ النَّعِيمِ."

"وَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ" (And He is the Mighty) is the one whom nothing overpowers and nothing defeats; He is able over a thing and its opposite, so He gives bliss to whom He wills and misery to whom He wills. "وَهُوَ الْحَكِيمُ" (And He is the Wise) does not will except what wisdom and justice require.

"تَرَوْنَها" (you see them): the pronoun in it refers to the heavens. It is a testimony by their seeing it, not a qualifier of "بِغَيْرِ عَمَدٍ" (without pillars), just as you say to your companion, "I am without a sword and without a spear, you see me." If you ask, "What is its place in i'rab (grammatical analysis)?" I answer: it has no place, because it is a new (resumptive) clause. Or it is in the genitive position as an attribute of "عَمَدٍ" (pillars), meaning: "without pillars that are seen," i.e. He has supported them with pillars that are not seen, and these are His holding them by His power.

"هذا" (this) is a reference to what was mentioned of His creations. "الخلق" (al-khalq) means the created thing (al-makhluq). "وَالَّذِينَ مِنْ دُونِهِ" (and those besides Him) are their gods. He rebuked them, showing that these great things are among what God created and brought into being: "فَأَرُونِي مَاذَا خَلَقَ الَّذِينَ مِنْ دُونِهِ" (show me what those besides Him have created), so that they might deserve worship in your eyes. Then He turned away from rebuking them to recording against them that they had plunged into an error beyond which there is no error.

He is Luqman ibn Ba'ura, the son of the sister of Ayyub (Job) or the son of his maternal aunt. It was said that he was among the descendants of Azar. He lived a thousand years and met Dawud (David), peace be upon him, and took knowledge from him. He used to give legal rulings (yufti) before Dawud was sent as a prophet, and when Dawud was sent, he stopped giving rulings. He was asked about this and said: "Shall I not be content when I have been relieved of it?" It was also said that he was a judge among the Children of Israel. Most of the reports hold that he was a sage (hakim) and not a prophet. From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Luqman was neither a prophet nor a king, but he was a black shepherd, and Allah granted him freedom, and accepted his words and his counsel, so his story is related in the Qur'an that you may follow his counsel." Ikrima and al-Sha'bi said: "He was a prophet." It was also said: "He was given the choice between prophethood and wisdom, and he chose wisdom." [Al-Zamakhshari mentioned in this regard the disagreement of the scholars about his prophethood, and mentioned in the course of it that he was given the choice between prophethood and wisdom and chose wisdom. Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: "In this there is a considerable distance, because wisdom is included within prophethood and is a drop from its sea, and the highest ranks of the wise fall short of the lowest ranks of the prophets by an immeasurable degree. It is not wise to choose wisdom divested of prophethood."] From Ibn al-Musayyib: he was a black man from the blacks of Egypt, a tailor. From Mujahid: he was a black slave with thick lips and cracked feet (mutashaqqiq al-qadamayn). [His saying "mutashaqqiq" in al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari): "al-shafaq" is the poor quality of things; one says "ghita' mushaffaq," meaning "of poor quality." The apparent reading is "mutashaqqiq" with two qaf. (ʿ)] It was also said that he was a carpenter, and it was said that he was a shepherd, and it was said that he used to gather a bundle of firewood for his master every day. It is also reported from him (Mujahid) that he said to a man who was looking at him: "If you see me with thick lips, then from between them comes forth gentle speech, and if you see me as black, then my heart is white." It is reported that a man stood over him in his assembly and said: "Are you not the one who used to graze with me in such-and-such a place?" He said: "Yes." The man said: "What has brought you to what I see?" He said: "Truthfulness in speech, and silence about what does not concern me." It is reported that he entered upon Dawud, peace be upon him, while he was weaving a coat of mail, and Allah had made the iron soft for him like clay. He wished to ask him, but wisdom overtook him and he remained silent. When Dawud finished it, he put it on and said: "You are indeed the garment of war." Luqman said: "Silence is wisdom, and few are those who practise it." Dawud said to him: "Truly you have been named a sage." It is reported that his master ordered him to slaughter a sheep and to bring out from it the two best morsels. He brought out the tongue and the heart. Then, after some days, he ordered him to do the same and to bring out the two worst morsels, and he brought out the tongue and the heart again. He was asked about this and said: "They are the best of things when they are good, and the worst of things when they are bad." From Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, that he said to a black man: "Do not grieve, for among the best of people were three from the blacks: Bilal, Mahja' the freedman of Umar, and Luqman." (Clause on "an") "An" here is the explanatory particle (al-mufassira), because the giving of wisdom carries the sense of saying. Allah, glory be to Him, has drawn attention to the fact that the original wisdom and the true knowledge are acting upon them, and worshipping Allah and thanking Him, since He explained the giving of wisdom as prompting to gratitude: ﴿Whoever gives thanks, gives thanks only for his own benefit; and whoever is ungrateful, then indeed Allah is ﴾ "ghaniyyun" (Self-sufficient), not in need of thanks, ﴿"hamid"﴾ (Praiseworthy), worthy to be praised even if no one praises Him.

It is said: the name of his son was "An'am." Al-Kalbi said it was "Ashkam." It is also said that his son and his wife were disbelievers, but he kept at them until they both embraced Islam. ﴿Indeed, associating others with Allah is a tremendous wrong﴾, because equating one from whom there is no blessing except that it comes from Him with one from whom there is no blessing at all, and from whom it is inconceivable that any blessing could come, is a wrong whose magnitude cannot be fathomed.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 31, verse 14–15:

[Al-Zamakhshari said:] "Her carrying him" means she bears him in weakness upon weakness, like your saying "رجع عودا على بدء" (raja'a 'awdan 'ala bad'), meaning "it returns the way it began." This is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The meaning is that she grows weak with a weakness upon a weakness, that is, her weakness increases and multiplies, because the more the pregnancy grows and becomes great, the more heavy and weak she becomes.

It is read: "wahnan 'ala wahnin" with the vowel on the second letter (wahanan), reported from Abu 'Amr. It is said: wahana yahinu and wahuna yahuna.

"And his weaning is in two years" — "Give thanks to Me and to your parents" is an explanation of "We enjoined upon man." "Of which you have no knowledge" — by negating knowledge of it he meant negating it itself, that is: do not associate with Me that which is not a thing. [Mahmud said: "Its meaning is: that which is not a thing, and he expressed the negation of the known by the negation of knowledge." Ahmad said: this is from the same category as his saying:

"On a dark road whose landmark is not followed"

meaning: that which has no divinity, so that you would have knowledge of its divinity. And it is not as he mentioned concerning Pharaoh's saying "I do not know for you any god other than me," whose meaning has passed earlier.]

He means the idols, as in His saying, "What they call upon besides Him is nothing" (see 31:? in the sense of "min shay'"). "Companion in goodness" (ma'rufan) means being a companion, or a good companion in kindness, with fine character, forbearance, tolerance, righteousness, and joining ties, and what generosity and manliness require. "And follow the way of one who turns to Me in repentance" — he means: follow the way of the believers in your religion, and do not follow their way in it, even though you are commanded to treat them well in this world. Then to Me is your return and their return, and I will reward you for your faith and reward them for their disbelief. This teaches the ruling of this world and what is obligatory upon a person in companionship and association with them: observing the right of parenthood and honoring it, and their due obligations which may not be neglected. Then it explains their ruling and state in the Hereafter.

It is related that it was revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and his mother. In the story: she remained three days without eating or drinking until they pried open her mouth with a stick [Qawlahu "hatta shajaru fahaha bi-'ud" — in al-Sihah: shajarahu bi-r-rumh, i.e. he stabbed him. (A)]. It is also related that he said: "If she had seventy souls and they came out one by one, I would not turn back to disbelief."

If you say: how does this statement come in the middle of Luqman's advice? I say: it is a parenthetical statement inserted by way of digression, to affirm what is in Luqman's advice of prohibition of shirk. If you say: how is "His mother bore him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years" inserted between the commentator and the commented? I say: when He enjoined the parents, He mentioned what the mother endures and suffers of hardships and toils in carrying and weaning him for this lengthy period, to make the enjoining of the mother especially obligatory [Mahmud said: "In it is the specification of the mother's right, which corresponds to its beginning, so mention of her in the obligation of goodness is in the transmitted hadith." Ahmad said: this is of the kind of what the jurists say: that the mother's labor is the child's work before puberty, and this serves to affirm her right, and God knows best.] and as a reminder of her great right, singled out. For this reason the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to the one who asked him, "Who is most deserving of my good companionship?": "Your mother, then your mother, then your mother," then after that said, "then your father [Related by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi from the hadith of Bahz ibn Hakim from his father from his grandfather, who said: "I said, O Messenger of God, who is most deserving...", the hadith; and it has a witness in the Two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Zur'a from Abu Hurayra who said: "A man came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: Who is most deserving of my companionship? — the hadith"]."

It is related of some Arabs that he carried his mother on his back to Hajj, while he himself recited in his chant:

"I carry my mother, and she is the one who carries me,
She nurses me with abundant milk and its remainder."

And "one who does not repay a parent for his deeds" [For an Arab who carries his mother to Hajj, "wa hiya al-hammala": a circumstantial clause, i.e., she is much carrying according to what she was, or it is her custom to do that; "tarda'uni" is an interposed circumstantial clause; "al-durra" with a damma: abundance of milk and its flowing, and what is meant by it is the abundant milk; "al-'alala" with a damma: the remainder of milk, the second milking, and it is applied to the remainder of a horse's run. "Al-'alal" is the second drink, and the first drink is "al-nahl." It is also related as "tarda'uni al-durra." "Al-fi'al" with a fatha: doing good; and by "walid" he meant the mother, or what includes both father and mother.]

If you say: what is the meaning of fixing the weaning at two years? I say: the meaning of fixing it at this period is that it is the limit which may not be exceeded, and the matter for less than two years is left to the mother's judgment: if she knows that he is strong enough to be weaned, she may wean him. This is indicated by His saying, "The mothers suckle their children for two full years, for whoever wishes to complete the nursing" (2:233). By this al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, cited that the period of nursing is two years, and that the establishment of milk-kinship is not valid after their expiry; this is the view of Abu Yusuf and Muhammad. As for Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, the period of nursing is thirty months. It is related from Abu Hanifa: if she weaned him before two years, and he became independent of milk by food, and then she nursed him, it is not nursing; and if he ate only weakly and was not independent of milk, and then she nursed him, it is nursing that establishes prohibition.

In the story: she remained three days without eating or drinking until they pried open her mouth with a stick [Qawlahu "hatta shajaru fahaha bi-'ud" — in al-Sihah: shajarahu bi-r-rumh, i.e. he stabbed him. (A)]. It is also related that he said: "If she had seventy souls and they came out one by one, I would not turn back to disbelief."

If you say: how does this statement come in the middle of Luqman's advice? I say: it is a parenthetical statement inserted by way of digression, to affirm what is in Luqman's advice of prohibition of shirk. If you say: how is "His mother bore him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years" inserted between the commentator and the commented? I say: when He enjoined the parents, He mentioned what the mother endures and suffers of hardships and toils in carrying and weaning him for this lengthy period, to make the enjoining of the mother especially obligatory [Mahmud said: "In it is the specification of the mother's right, which corresponds to its beginning, so mention of her in the obligation of goodness is in the transmitted hadith." Ahmad said: this is of the kind of what the jurists say: that the mother's labor is the child's work before puberty, and this serves to affirm her right, and God knows best.] and as a reminder of her great right, singled out. For this reason the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to the one who asked him, "Who is most deserving of my good companionship?": "Your mother, then your mother, then your mother," then after that said, "then your father [Related by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi from the hadith of Bahz ibn Hakim from his father from his grandfather, who said: "I said, O Messenger of God, who is most deserving...", the hadith; and it has a witness in the Two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Zur'a from Abu Hurayra who said: "A man came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: Who is most deserving of my companionship? — the hadith"]."

It is related of some Arabs that he carried his mother on his back to Hajj, while he himself recited in his chant:

"I carry my mother, and she is the one who carries me,
She nurses me with abundant milk and its remainder."

And "one who does not repay a parent for his deeds" [For an Arab who carries his mother to Hajj, "wa hiya al-hammala": a circumstantial clause, i.e., she is much carrying according to what she was, or it is her custom to do that; "tarda'uni" is an interposed circumstantial clause; "al-durra" with a damma: abundance of milk and its flowing, and what is meant by it is the abundant milk; "al-'alala" with a damma: the remainder of milk, the second milking, and it is applied to the remainder of a horse's run. "Al-'alal" is the second drink, and the first drink is "al-nahl." It is also related as "tarda'uni al-durra." "Al-fi'al" with a fatha: doing good; and by "walid" he meant the mother, or what includes both father and mother.]

If you say: what is the meaning of fixing the weaning at two years? I say: the meaning of fixing it at this period is that it is the limit which may not be exceeded, and the matter for less than two years is left to the mother's judgment: if she knows that he is strong enough to be weaned, she may wean him. This is indicated by His saying, "The mothers suckle their children for two full years, for whoever wishes to complete the nursing" (2:233). By this al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, cited that the period of nursing is two years, and that the establishment of milk-kinship is not valid after their expiry; this is the view of Abu Yusuf and Muhammad. As for Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, the period of nursing is thirty months. It is related from Abu Hanifa: if she weaned him before two years, and he became independent of milk by food, and then she nursed him, it is not nursing; and if he ate only weakly and was not independent of milk, and then she nursed him, it is nursing that establishes prohibition.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 31, verse 16:

It is read as "mithqala habbatin" with both the accusative (naṣb) and the nominative (raf'). According to the accusative reading, the pronoun refers to the (small) deed (al-hanah) of good or evil [[Al-hanah: in al-Sihah, under h-n: "on the pattern of akh, it is a word of reference; its meaning is 'a thing,' and its feminine is hanah." Al-qama'a: smallness and insignificance. Thus in al-Sihah (ʿ)]]. The meaning is: if it is small and insignificant like a mustard seed, yet, despite its smallness, it is in the most hidden and most secure place, such as the inside of a rock [[Mahmud said: "This is from the rhetorical device called al-tatmim." Ahmad said: he means that he completed its description by the obscurity of its place within the rock, and this is in the vein of her saying, "as if he were a lamp upon its head."]], or wherever it may be, in the upper or lower world, Allah will bring it on the Day of Resurrection and will call its doer to account for it. Indeed, Allah is Subtle (latif), whose knowledge reaches every hidden thing, All-Aware (khabir), who knows its essence.

It is narrated from Qatadah: "Subtle" means in extracting it, and "All-Aware" means in knowing its place of rest.

According to the nominative reading, the pronoun is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamir al-qiṣṣa), and the word "mithqal" is feminine only because it is added to "habbah," as in the verse:

"As the spear-shaft is reddened by blood" [[The explanation of this evidence was given earlier in the first volume, page 395, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

It is narrated that the son of Luqman said to him: "Do you see that a grain is in the depths of the sea—that is, in its diving places—does Allah know it?" He said: "Indeed Allah knows the smallest things in the most hidden places, for a grain in a rock is more hidden than it is in water."

It is said that the rock is the one beneath the earth, and it is Sijjin, where the deeds of the disbelievers are recorded. It is also read as "fatakun" with a kasra on the kaf, from "wakana al-ta'ir yakinu," meaning when a bird settles in its nest, which is its resting place at night.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 31, verse 17:

﴿And be patient over what befalls you.﴾ It may be general, covering every trial that befalls him, and it may be specific, covering the harm that befalls him in enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong: the harm from those whom he stirs toward good and who object to his rebuking them for evil. ﴿Indeed, that is of the matters ordained by God (min 'azm Allah min al-umur)﴾, meaning: decreed as an obligation and a binding requirement. From this is the hadith, "There is no fast for one who does not resolve (yu'azzim) to fast from the night" [[Mentioned previously in al-Baqarah.]], meaning he has not firmly decided it by intention. Do you not see his saying, peace be upon him, "for one who does not make the fast a night-time resolution" [[Also mentioned previously.]]? From this also is "God loves that His concessions be taken just as He loves that His obligations be upheld" [[Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn 'Adi through the route of Abu Salamah from Abu Hurayrah: "A man said, 'O Messenger of God, shall I shorten the prayer during my journey?' He said, 'Yes, indeed God loves that His concession be taken just as He loves that His obligation be taken.'" In its chain is 'Umar ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Khash'am al-Yamami, who is munkar al-hadith, as stated by Ibn 'Adi. He also narrated it through the route of Sa'd ibn Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id, who said: my brother 'Abd Allah narrated to me from his father that Abu Hurayrah, raising it (to the Prophet), said something similar. Ibn Hibban, Ahmad, al-Bazzar, and Abu Ya'la related it from the narration of Harb ibn Qays from Nafi' from Ibn 'Umar with the wording: "God loves that His concessions be availed of just as He loves that His obligations be availed of." On this subject there is also a report from Ibn 'Abbas, narrated by Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah through the narration of Hisham ibn Hassan from 'Ikrimah from him, with the wording of Ibn 'Umar. And from Ibn Mas'ud, narrated by al-Tabarani, al-'Uqayli, and Abu Nu'aym through the narration of Mu'ammar ibn 'Abd Allah al-Ansari from Shu'bah from al-Hakam from Ibrahim from 'Alqamah from him; Mu'ammar alone related it as a marfu' report, while Ghundar, Rawh ibn 'Ubadah, and others related it from Shu'bah as a mawquf report. It was narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah and others. And from 'A'ishah: narrated by Ibn 'Adi through the narration of al-Hakam ibn 'Abd Allah al-Ayli from al-Qasim from 'A'ishah, and through the narration of 'Umar ibn 'Ubayd al-Basri from Hisham from his father from her; al-Hakam and 'Umar are both weak. It was also narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Awsat through the route of Isma'il ibn 'Isa al-'Attar: 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Jabbar narrated to us, 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd ibn Adam narrated to us from Abu al-Darda', Abu Umamah, Wathilah, and Anas, with it; he said: it is not related except through this chain, and Isma'il alone transmitted it. I say: the chain is unknown (majhul).]] His saying, "and their saying, 'a resolve (azmah) from the resolves of our Lord'" is a fragment of a hadith narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ahmad, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi through the narration of Bahz ibn Hakim from his father from his grandfather, within the course of his hadith, in which he said, "And whoever withholds it, meaning the zakah, we shall take it and half his wealth as a resolve from the resolves of our Lord; it is not for the family of Muhammad to have any share of it." Its chain is sound (hasan).]]

And their saying: "a resolve from the resolves of our Lord." From this also: "the resolves of kings" (azamat al-muluk). That is when a king says to one of those under his authority: "I have bound you (azamtu 'alayka) to do such-and-such," and when he says that, the one so bound has no alternative to doing it and no leeway to abandon it.

Its real sense is that it is a case of naming the object by the verbal noun (tasmiyat al-maf'ul bi'l-masdar), its origin being "ma'zumat al-umur," meaning the things that are firmly determined and enjoined. It may also be a verbal noun in the sense of the agent: its origin being "'azimat al-umur," from the Exalted's saying, ﴿Then when the matter is resolved (fa-idha 'azama al-amr)﴾, like your saying: "jadda al-amr" (the matter became serious) and "sadaqa al-qital" (the fighting was true). Sufficient is this verse as an indication of the antiquity of these acts of obedience, that they were enjoined upon the earlier nations as well, and that prayer has always been of great standing, of ancient precedence over all else, and enjoined in all religions.

Tusa'ir and tusa'ir (with and without the shadda, i.e. tusa'ʿir and tuṣaʿʿir): it is said "aṣʿara khaddahu", "ṣaʿʿarahu" and "ṣāʿarahu", like your saying "aʿlāhu", "ʿallāhu" and "ʿālāhu": they have the same meaning. Al-ṣaʿr (and al-ṣaydd) is a disease that afflicts the camel, from which its neck is twisted. The meaning is: turn your face toward people in humility, and do not turn your cheek and side away from them, as the arrogant do. He intends:

﴿And do not walk in the earth exultantly﴾, or he has placed the verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier, meaning "exultantly" (marahan). It is also permissible that he intends: "Do not walk for the sake of exultation and insolence", i.e. let not your aim in walking be idleness and insolence, as many people walk for that purpose, and not for the fulfilment of a religious or worldly need. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿And be not like those who went forth from their homes insolently and to be seen of people﴾. The one who struts (al-mukhtāl) is the counterpart of the one who walks exultantly, and likewise the boastful (al-fakhūr) is the counterpart of the one who turns his cheek away out of pride. ﴿And be moderate in your pace﴾: be just in it, so that your walk is between two walks: do not trudge like the feeble-hearted, nor leap like the vigorous. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hastening in walking takes away the radiance of the believer." [This has come from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, Abu Sa'id and Ibn 'Umar. Ibn 'Adi narrated it through the transmission of 'Ammar ibn Mutarrad, who is abandoned (matrūk), and al-Walid ibn Muslim followed him, though he is weaker than him; but he said: "from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from al-Mughirah, from Abu Sa'id and al-Walid ibn Salamah." There is another chain for it, narrated by Ibn 'Adi through his transmission from 'Amr ibn Sahban, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, and Abu Nu'aym narrated it in al-Hilyah by way of Abu Ma'shar, from Sa'id, from Abu Hurayrah, and its chain is also weak.] As for the saying of 'A'ishah about 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both): "When he walked, he hastened," she only meant a pace elevated above the trudging of the feeble-hearted. [Ibn al-Athir mentioned it in al-Nihayah. I say: perhaps he took it from al-Fa'iq. In Ibn Sa'd's al-Tabaqat, through the transmission of Sulayman ibn Abi Hathmah, who said: Al-Shifa' bint 'Abd Allah, the mother of Sulayman, said: "When 'Umar walked..." and he mentioned it.]

It has been read "wa-aqsid" with a hamzah (aqṣid), meaning: be direct in your walk, from "aqṣada al-rāmī", when the archer aims his arrow straight toward the target. ﴿And lower your voice﴾: reduce it, diminish it and shorten it, from your saying: "Fulan yaghuḍḍu min Fulān", when he belittles him and lowers his standing. ﴿Surely the most hideous of voices﴾: the most frightening and repugnant of them, from your saying: "shay' nukr", when people find something unfamiliar and are repelled and repulsed by it. The donkey is a figure of eloquent disparagement and abuse, and so is its bray. Because of their revulsion at mentioning it plainly and their avoidance of its name, they use euphemisms for it and shun explicit mention of it, saying "the one with long ears," just as they euphemize disgusting things. It has been counted among the blameworthy manners that the donkey be mentioned in a gathering of people of honour and dignity. Some Arabs refuse to ride a donkey out of disdain, even if walking on foot wearies them, [his saying "minhu al-rijlah" means: walking on foot, i.e. even if walking and not riding exhausts him. In al-Sihah, "al-rajl" with a fatha on the ra' is the verbal noun of your saying "rajila", meaning he remained on foot. (ʿ)] So the likening of those who raise their voices to donkeys, and the depiction of their voices as braying, is a removal of the word of comparison from the speech and its presentation in the form of metaphor, since they are made donkeys and their voice braying, together with intense exaggeration in disparagement and vilification, and an excessive discouraging from raising the voice and an encouragement away from it, and a warning that it is in a place of Allah's dislike. If you ask: why is "the voice of the donkeys" in the singular and not the plural? I say: it is not intended that the voice of each individual member of this species be mentioned so that it would be plural; rather, the intent is that every species of speaking animal has a voice, and the most hideous of the voices of these species is the voice of this species, so it was necessary to make it singular.

What is in the heavens: the sun, the moon, the stars, the clouds, and other things; and what is in the earth: the seas, the rivers, the minerals, the animals, and what cannot be counted. "Asbagha" (He has bestowed abundantly) is also read with the sīn and the ṣād (as asbagha/aṣbagha); and so is every sīn that is followed by a ghayn, a khāʾ, or a qāf: you say salakha / ṣalakha (to strip off), and in saqar / ṣaqar, and in sāligh / ṣāligh [[The author's words "and in sāligh, ṣāligh": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: salagha the cow or the sheep, when it drops the tooth that replaces the incisor (al-sadīs), and al-salūgh is said of cloven-hoofed animals in the same way as al-buzūl is said of those with pads. (ʿ)]]. It is also read: niʿmah, niʿmatan, and niʿmatuhu.

If you ask: what is a blessing (niʿmah)? I answer: every benefit intended as a kindness. God Most High created the entire world as a blessing, for it is either a living being or a non-living thing. What is not living is a blessing to living beings, and the living being is a blessing in that its being brought into existence as alive is a blessing upon it, for were it not for its being brought into existence as alive, benefit from it would not be valid, and everything that leads to benefit and makes it valid is a blessing.

If you ask: why was the creation of the world intended as a kindness? I answer: because He creates nothing except for a purpose, otherwise it would be pointless (ʿabath), and futility is not permissible for Him; nor is it permissible that the purpose should return to Him in the form of some benefit, since He is self-sufficient, not in need of benefits. So nothing remains except that the purpose returns to the living beings, namely their benefit.

If you ask: what is the meaning of "apparent" (ẓāhirah) and "hidden" (bāṭinah)? I answer: the apparent is whatever is known through observation, and the hidden is what is known only through proof, or is not known at all. How many blessings are in the human body which he does not know, and is not guided to knowing. People have said much on this:

From Mujāhid: the apparent is the manifestation of Islam and victory over the enemies, and the hidden is the reinforcements from the angels. From al-Ḥasan, may God be pleased with him: the apparent is Islam, and the hidden is concealment (of sins). From al-Ḍaḥḥāk: the apparent is beauty of form, height of stature, and the proportion of the limbs; and the hidden is knowledge (maʿrifah).

It has also been said: the apparent is sight, hearing, the tongue, and the rest of the outward limbs; and the hidden is the heart, the intellect, understanding, and what is similar to these.

It is reported in the supplication of Mūsā, peace be upon him: "My God, guide me to the most hidden of Your blessings upon Your servants." He said: "The most hidden of My blessings upon them is the soul (nafs)." It is also reported: the least of what the people of the Fire will be punished with is being made to take their breaths (al-akhdh bi-l-anfās) [[I have not found it.]].
Its meaning: "Would they follow them even though the Shaytan is calling them", that is, while the Shaytan is calling them to the punishment.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 31, verse 22:

It is read by ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu): "wa-man yuslim" with the doubled sin (yusallim, i.e., the intensive form). It is said: "aslama amrahu" and "sallama amrahu ilā Allāh." If you ask: why is it transitive with "ilā" here, when it is transitive with "lām" in His words, "Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah" (﴿بَلَىٰ مَنْ أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُ لِلَّهِ﴾)? I say:

Its meaning with "lām" is that He made his face, which is his essence and self, sound (sālim) for Allah, that is, sincerely (khāliṣan) for Him. Its meaning with "ilā" is that he handed over his self to Him, as goods are handed over to a man when they are delivered to him. The intended sense is reliance upon Him and committing oneself to Him. ﴿فَقَدِ اسْتَمْسَكَ بِالْعُرْوَةِ الْوُثْقَىٰ﴾ is by way of illustration (min bāb al-tamthīl): the state of the one who relies (al-mutawakkil) is likened to the state of one who wishes to lower himself from a high cliff, so he takes precaution for himself by grasping the strongest handhold of a sturdy rope, trusted not to break. ﴿وَإِلَى اللَّهِ عَاقِبَةُ الْأُمُورِ﴾: that is, all matters ultimately return to Him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 31, verses 23–24:

It is read "yuhzinka" and "yahzunka," from "hazina" and "ahzana." The widely used form is "ahzanahu" and "yahzunuhu." The meaning: do not let the disbelief of those who disbelieve, and their plotting against Islam, grieve you, for Allah, mighty and majestic, will repel their plotting back into their own faces, will take vengeance on them, and will punish them for their deeds. ﴿Indeed, Allah knows what is in the breasts of His servants﴾, so He will deal with them according to what He knows. ﴿We will let them enjoy themselves for a little while with their worldly life; then We will compel them to a severe punishment.﴾ The compulsion of them to punishment and their being driven to it is likened to the compulsion of one who is forced toward something from which he cannot escape [[Mahmud said: "The compulsion to punishment is likened to the compulsion of one who is forced toward something from which he cannot escape." Ahmad said:

The explanation of this compulsion in the hadith is that, because of the severity of what they suffer from the Fire, they seek coolness, so Allah sends down the zamharir (bitter cold) upon them. It then becomes for them like the intensity of blazing flame, so they wish for the flame to return, out of compulsion. This is a report of compulsion. And upon the threads of this eloquence Al-Kindi held when he said:

They see death before them and behind them... so they choose, while death is compulsion.]] from him. "Ghalizh" (severe) is a metaphor drawn from thick bodies. What is meant is intensity and heaviness upon the one being punished.

Say, "Praise belongs to Allah." Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 31, verse 28:

﴿Except as a single soul﴾ — that is, creating and resurrecting it is no different, with respect to His power, whether it is little or much, one or many; there is no disparity. This is because disparity would only arise if the creation of a single soul, or of many souls, were such that one matter occupied Him from another matter, and one act from another act. But He is exalted above that. ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing﴾, who hears every sound and sees everything seen in a single state, with the perception of some of them not preoccupying Him from the perception of others. Likewise, the creation and the resurrection.

Each of the sun and the moon runs in its orbit, and [each] traverses it until a known time: the sun until the end of the year, and the moon until the end of the month. It is related from al-Hasan: "The appointed term (al-ajal al-musamma) is the Day of Resurrection, because their running does not cease except then."

[The verses] also indicate, by the night and the day, their succession, their lengthening and shortening, and the running of the two luminaries in their orbits, that all of this is by determination and reckoning; and, by His encompassing of all the deeds of creation, [they indicate] the greatness of His power and wisdom.

If you say: "[The verb] yajri li-ajalin musamman (runs for a named term) and yajri ila ajalin musamman (runs until a named term): is it an interchange of the two particles?" I say: No. Only one of dull nature and narrow stable (ḍayyiq al-ʿaṭn) would take this path. [Note by the commentator: his saying "only one of dull nature and narrow stable" — in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: it is the place where camels kneel at the water, so that they may drink, [then] return to drink again.] Rather, the two meanings, namely the sense of reaching a limit (intihāʾ) and the sense of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ), are each suited to the soundness of the purpose. For your saying yajri ila ajalin musamman means: it reaches it and arrives at it. And your saying yajri li-ajalin musamman means: it runs in order to attain a named term, making the running specific to attaining a named term. Do you not see that the running of the sun is specific to the end of the year, and the running of the moon is specific to the end of the month? Thus both meanings are not out of place here, [in the context of] that which is described of the wonders of His power and wisdom, which the living, capable, knowing beings cannot achieve. How then [could one worship] the inanimate object that you invoke besides God? It is only because He is the Truth, whose divinity is established, and that whatever is besides Him has false divinity. "And that God is the Most High, the Great" — exalted in majesty and dominion. Or: that which has been revealed to you of these signs [is revealed] to explain that God is the Truth, that any god other than Him is false, and that God is the Most High, the Great, above being associated with.

It is recited as *al-fulk* (الفلك), with a ḍammah on the lām. Every *fiʿl* (فِعل, the pattern of the root's middle vowel) may take the form *fuʿl* (فُعل), just as any *fiʿl* may take the form *fiʿl*, according to the principle of *taʿwīḍ* (compensation, substituting one element for another). As for *bi-niʿmāt Allāh* (بنِعمات الله), it is recited with a sukūn on the ʿayn. The ʿayn of the pattern *fiʿalāt* may be read with a fatḥah, a kasrah, or a sukūn.

﴿By the favour of Allah﴾ (بنِعْمَتِ اللَّهِ): by His kindness and His mercy. ﴿Patient﴾ (صَبَّارٍ): in the face of His trials. ﴿Grateful﴾ (شَكُورٍ): for His blessings. These two are the two attributes of the believer, so it is as if He said: "Indeed, in that are signs for every believer."

The waves rise and pile up, so that they become like shades (*zulal*). A *zulla* is anything that overshadows you, such as a mountain, a cloud, or other things. It was also read as *kaz-zilal*, the plural of *zulla*, like *qilla* and *qilal*.

﴿Among them is a moderate one﴾: moderate in disbelief and wrongdoing, one who has been restrained from his excess and has been checked to some degree. Or, moderate in the sincerity he had at sea, meaning that this sincerity which arises at the time of fear does not remain for anyone at all, and the moderate one is rare and scarce. It has also been said: he is a believer who remained steadfast in what he pledged to God at sea.

*Al-khatr* is the most extreme treachery. From it comes their saying: "You will not extend to us a span of treachery except that we will extend to you a fathom of *khatr*." The poet said:

"Even if you saw Abu 'Umayr, you would fill your hands with treachery and deceit."

*Al-ghadr* is the most extreme form of *khatr*.

It is narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw a man counting on the fingers of his right hand: "Glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, God is greatest, and there is no power nor strength except in God, the Most High, the Mighty," and on the fingers of his left hand: "O God, forgive me, have mercy on me, guide me, provide for me, and make me whole." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "You have filled your hands with good."

Here the intelligible is likened to the sensible by way of implicit metaphor (*al-makniyya*). "Filling the hands" is *takhyil* (imaginative representation). Both hands are mentioned because the man counted with them. The poet took him as an example for the state of Abu 'Umayr and of whoever sees him, by way of a sarcastic metaphorical analogy (*al-isti'ara al-tamthiliyya al-tahakkumiyya*). Whoever sees him and counts his faults is as if he has filled his hands with evil, not good. The counting is omitted to indicate that merely seeing him achieves this.

﴿لا يَجْزِي﴾: لا يُقضى عنه شيئًا. ومنه قيل للمتقاضي: المتجازي. وفي الحديث في جذعة ابن نيار: «تُجزى عنك ولا تُجزى عن أحد بعدك» [[تقدم في أوائل البقرة.]]. وقُرئ: ﴿لا يُجزئ﴾: لا يُغني [[قوله «وقرئ لا يجزئ لا يغنى» لعله: أي لا يغنى. (ع)]]. يقال: أجزأت عنك مجزأ فلان. والمعنى: لا يُجزى فيه، فحُذف.

﴿الْغَرُورُ﴾ الشيطان. وقيل: الدنيا. وقيل: تمنيكم في المعصية المغفرة. وعن سعيد بن جبير رضي الله عنه: الغِرّة بالله أن يتمادى الرجل في المعصية ويتمنى على الله المغفرة. وقيل: ذكرك لحسناتك ونسيانك لسيئاتك غِرّة.

وقُرئ بضم الغين، وهو مصدر غرّه غرورًا، وجُعل الغرور غارًّا، كما قيل: جدّ جدّه. أو أُريد زينة الدنيا لأنها غرور. فإن قلت: قوله ﴿وَلا مَوْلُودٌ هُوَ جازٍ عَنْ والِدِهِ شَيْئًا﴾ وارد على طريق من التوكيد لم يرد عليه ما هو معطوف [[قال محمود: «إن قلت: لم أكّد الجملة الثانية دون الأولى؟ قلت: لأن أكثر المسلمين كان آباؤهم قد ماتوا على الكفر، فلما كان إغناء الكافر عن المسلم بعيدًا لم يحتج تأكيدًا، ولما كان إغناء المسلم عن الكافر قد يقع في الأوهام أكّد نفيه» قال أحمد: وهذا الجواب تتوقف صحته على أن هذا الخطاب كان خاصًا بالموجودين حينئذ، والصحيح أنه عام لهم ولكل من ينطلق عليه اسم الناس، فالجواب المعتبر- والله أعلم- أن الله تعالى لما أكّد الوصية على الآباء، وقرن شكرهم بوجوب شكره عز وجل، وأوجب على الولد أن يكفي والده ما يسوءه بحسب نهاية إمكانه قطع هاهنا وهم الوالد في أن يكون الولد في القيامة مجزيه بحقه عليه، ويكفيه ما يلقاه من أهوال القيامة كما أوجب الله عليه في الدنيا ذلك في حقه، فلما كان إجزاء الولد عن الوالد مظنون الوقوع- لأن الله حضه عليه في الدنيا- كان جديرًا بتأكيد النفي لإزالة هذا الوهم، ولا كذلك العكس، فهذا جواب كافٍ شافٍ للعليل، إن شاء الله تعالى.]] عليه. قلت: الأمر كذلك، لأن الجملة الاسمية آكد من الفعلية، وقد انضم إلى ذلك قوله ﴿هُوَ﴾ وقوله ﴿مَوْلُودٌ﴾. والسبب في مجيئه على هذا السنن: أن الخطاب للمؤمنين وعليتهم [[قوله «وعليتهم» أي أشرافهم وعظماؤهم. (ع)]]: قبض آباؤهم على الكفر وعلى الدين الجاهلي، فأُريد حسم أطماعهم وأطماع الناس فيهم: أن ينفعوا آباءهم في الآخرة، وأن يشفعوا لهم، وأن يغنوا عنهم من الله شيئًا، فلذلك جيء به على الطريق الآكد. ومعنى التوكيد في لفظ ﴿مَوْلُودٌ﴾: أن الواحد منهم لو شفع للأب الأدنى الذي وُلد منه، لم تُقبل شفاعته، فضلًا أن يشفع لمن فوقه من أجداده، لأن الولد يقع على الولد وولد الولد، بخلاف المولود فإنه لمن وُلد منك.

A man from Muharib, who was al-Harith ibn Amr ibn Harithah, came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, tell me when the Hour will come. I have sown my seeds in the ground, but the sky has delayed its rain for us, so when will it rain? Tell me about my wife. She has conceived what is in her womb: will it be male or female? I know what I knew yesterday, so what will I do tomorrow? I know where I was born, so where will I die?" [Al-Wahidi and al-Tha'labi mention this without a chain of narration. Al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim narrate it through Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid, who said: "A man from the desert people came and said, 'O Muhammad, my wife is pregnant, so tell me when she will give birth,' and so on."] Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah has with Him the knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain, and He knows what is in the wombs. No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Aware.﴾

It is also reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The keys of the unseen are five," and he recited this verse. [Al-Bukhari narrated it from the hadith of Ibn Umar.]

It is reported from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "Whoever claims to know these five has lied. Beware of soothsaying (kahanah, the claim to know hidden matters), for soothsaying leads to polytheism (shirk, associating partners with God), and polytheism and its people are in the Fire."

It is reported from al-Mansur that he was troubled by wanting to know the length of his life. He saw in a dream as if a shape had extended its hand out of the sea and pointed to him with five fingers. He asked the scholars about it, and they interpreted it as five years, or five months, or other things, until Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, said: "Its interpretation is that the keys of the unseen are five, which no one knows except God, and what you seek to know has no path for you to it: ﴿with Him is the knowledge of the Hour﴾, its appointed time, ﴿and He sends down the rain﴾ in its season without advance or delay, and in a land it does not pass beyond. ﴿And He knows what is in the wombs﴾, male or female, complete or incomplete, and likewise whatever else of these conditions. ﴿And no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow﴾, good or evil. A pious soul may intend good and then do evil, and a sinful soul may intend evil and then do good. ﴿And no soul knows in what land it will die﴾. A soul may settle in a land, drive its tent pegs into it, and say, 'I will not leave it and I will be buried in it,' and then be cast by the arrows of destiny until it dies in a place it never imagined and its assumptions never suggested."

It is narrated that the Angel of Death passed by Solomon and began looking at a man among his companions, gazing at him for a long time. The man asked, "Who is this?" He was told, "The Angel of Death." The man said, "It seems he wants me." So Solomon asked that the man be carried on the wind and set down in the land of India, and this was done. Then the Angel of Death said to Solomon: "My constant gazing at him was out of amazement, because I had been commanded to take his soul in India, and he was with you."

[This is a statement attributed to a Companion (mawquf). Ahmad narrated it in al-Zuhd, and Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated it, both saying: Abd Allah ibn Numayr narrated to us from al-A'mash from Khaythamah from Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: "The Angel of Death entered..." and so on.]

Knowledge belongs to God, and awareness (diraya, knowing by one's own effort and reasoning) belongs to the servant, because awareness carries the meaning of scheming and cunning. The meaning is: the soul does not know, even if it employs its stratagems, what attaches to it and is specific to it and does not go beyond it. Nothing is more specific to a person than his earning and his final outcome. So if there is no way for him to know these two, then knowing anything else is even more remote.

It is also read: "bi-ayyi ardin" (in which land). Sibawayh compared the feminine form of ayy (which) to the feminine form of kull (all) in their saying: "kulatuhunna" (all of them, feminine).

It is narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah Luqman, Luqman will be his companion on the Day of Resurrection, and he will be given ten good deeds for every person who acted upon what is right and forbade what is wrong." [Al-Tha'labi, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Wahidi narrated it with their chains from Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]
